# Key passages — The Handbook of Careful Practice (invented for testing)

These passages are fictional. They exist only so the pipeline's tests and smoke runs
have a target that depends on no real tradition.

## HCP 1.1 — On acting before understanding
The carpenter who measures once and cuts twice blames the wood. Before you decide,
name aloud what you do not yet know, and say how long it would take to find out.
Haste that skips this step is not decisiveness; it is a wager placed with someone
else's money.

## HCP 1.4 — On the smallest sufficient action
When a fault appears, do the least that will actually repair it, and do that fully.
The one who tears down the whole wall to replace one brick has not been thorough;
they have been unwilling to judge which brick was loose.

## HCP 2.2 — On telling someone what they will not want to hear
Say the difficult thing early, in private, and once. To say it late is to have let
the harm grow for your own comfort. To say it publicly is to make the other person
defend themselves instead of hear you. To say it repeatedly is to want the feeling
of having said it.

## HCP 2.7 — On promises already made
A promise made in ignorance still binds until it is renegotiated with the person
who relied on it. You may not simply discover that the promise was unwise and treat
that discovery as a release. Go back to them, say what you now know, and ask.

## HCP 3.3 — On costs that fall on people who are not in the room
Count the cost to those who will not be asked and cannot object. A decision that
looks balanced among those present is usually unbalanced once they are counted.
